This hands-on experience fosters a more nuanced understanding of scientific inquiry, enabling citizens to critically evaluate scientific findings and engage in informed discussions about the implications of research. Furthermore, citizen science projects promote a sense of ownership and agency among participants, who feel empowered to contribute to the scientific enterprise and make a tangible difference in their communities.

Structured code review plays a pivotal role in enhancing the quality of software produced by engineering teams. One of the primary benefits of code review is that it enables reviewers to catch defects before the software is released, which significantly reduces the cost of fixing these defects. When defects are identified during the review process, they can be addressed immediately, resulting in far cheaper fixes compared to identifying and resolving them in production. This approach not only saves time and resources but also prevents the propagation of defects, which can have a ripple effect on the entire software system.

Another significant advantage of structured code review is that it facilitates knowledge sharing and reduces reliance on single experts within the team. When team members review each other's changes, they gain a deeper understanding of the codebase, its architecture, and the design decisions that have been made. This shared knowledge not only enhances the team's collective expertise but also empowers team members to make informed decisions and contribute to the codebase with greater confidence. As a result, the team becomes less dependent on individual experts, promoting a more collaborative and self-sufficient environment.

Regular code review also serves as a powerful enforcer of consistent coding standards, making the software easier to maintain over time. When team members review each other's code, they are more likely to adhere to established coding conventions, coding styles, and best practices. This uniformity in coding standards ensures that the software is more predictable, easier to navigate, and less prone to errors. Moreover, the consistent application of coding standards makes it easier for new team members to join and become familiar with the codebase, reducing the learning curve and accelerating the development process. By enforcing consistent coding standards through regular review, teams can lay the foundation for a maintainable and scalable software system.

In high-stakes professions such as aviation and surgery, written checklists are a crucial tool in reducing preventable errors. One key advantage of checklists is that they reduce reliance on memory for routine but critical steps, particularly when individuals are under stress or fatigue. In these professions, attention to detail is paramount, and even minor oversights can have catastrophic consequences. Checklists provide a clear, step-by-step guide that ensures all necessary procedures are performed, thereby minimizing the risk of human error. By referencing a written checklist, individuals can focus on executing the tasks rather than trying to recall them, which can be especially challenging in high-pressure situations.

Another benefit of written checklists is that they standardize communication within teams by providing a defined moment for team members to raise concerns. In the chaos of a high-stakes operation, it's easy for important details to be overlooked or dismissed. A checklist provides a structured framework for discussing and addressing potential issues, ensuring that everyone is on the same page. This standardized communication helps prevent misunderstandings and ensures that all team members are aware of the plan and any potential risks. By giving every team member a clear moment to voice concerns, checklists promote a culture of transparency and accountability.

Documented results demonstrate the effectiveness of written checklists in reducing complications in high-stakes professions. The World Health Organization's surgical safety checklist, for example, has shown measurable reductions in complications after its adoption. This checklist is designed to be used before, during, and after surgery to ensure that patients receive the best possible care. By incorporating a checklist into their workflow, healthcare professionals can identify potential risks and take proactive steps to mitigate them, resulting in better patient outcomes. In aviation, similar checklists are used to ensure that pilots and air traffic controllers follow standardized procedures, reducing the risk of errors and improving safety.

Improvements in weather forecasting over recent decades have produced significant economic value. One of the key beneficiaries of these advancements is the agricultural sector, particularly farmers. More accurate forecasts enable them to time planting, irrigation, and harvesting with greater precision, thereby reducing crop losses and increasing overall productivity. This is because precise weather information allows farmers to avoid planting during unfavorable conditions, reduce water usage during periods of drought, and harvest crops when they are at their optimal ripeness, minimizing the risk of spoilage and damage. As a result, the economic value of improved weather forecasting is evident in the increased yields and reduced losses that farmers experience.

The notion that causation can be reduced to mere regular succession between types of events is an oversimplification that fails to capture the complexities of causal relationships. Regularity accounts, which attempt to define causation solely in terms of the frequency of predictable outcomes following specific types of events, are unable to distinguish genuine causal relations from accidental or common-cause correlations. For instance, a falling barometer reading is regularly followed by a storm, yet it does not cause the storm. This is because the storm's occurrence is also correlated with other factors, such as atmospheric pressure and wind patterns, which are not causally related to the falling barometer reading. The regularity of this succession is thus coincidental rather than causal.

In contrast, interventionist accounts, developed by philosophers such as James Woodward, offer a more nuanced understanding of causation by identifying causal relations with dependencies that remain invariant under ideal interventions on the putative cause. An ideal intervention involves manipulating the cause in a way that isolates its effect, allowing us to determine whether the cause is indeed responsible for the effect. This approach highlights the importance of considering the causal mechanisms and dependencies that underlie the relationship between events, rather than simply counting the frequency of predictable outcomes. By focusing on the invariant dependencies that remain after intervening on the cause, we can distinguish genuine causal relations from accidental correlations.

The interventionist account also explains the epistemic privilege of randomized controlled experiments, which are widely regarded as the gold standard of scientific research. These experiments involve manipulating the putative cause in a way that severs it from its ordinary antecedents, allowing researchers to isolate the causal effect. By designing experiments that approximate ideal interventions, scientists can establish causal relationships with greater confidence, as the effect is no longer influenced by extraneous factors that might be correlated with the cause. In this sense, the interventionist account provides a theoretical framework for understanding the epistemic privilege of randomized controlled experiments, which is essential for establishing causal knowledge in various fields of study.

Analyzing biological function in etiological terms offers a more comprehensive understanding of its underlying mechanisms and normative dimensions compared to purely causal-role accounts. Selected-effect accounts, which pinpoint a trait's function with the effect for which its ancestors were selected, provide a nuanced explanation of the normativity of function, encompassing the possibility of malfunction. This is a distinctive feature that a purely dispositional analysis, focused on the trait's current causal role, cannot accommodate. By delving into the evolutionary history of a trait, selected-effect accounts reveal why a particular function is attributed to it, highlighting the adaptive significance that underpins its presence.

In contrast, causal-role accounts following Cummins' seminal work struggle to distinguish a trait's function from its accidental effects without relativizing function to the explanatory interests of the investigator. This relativization undermines the objectivity of functional attribution, as it implies that function is dependent on the observer's perspective rather than being an inherent property of the trait itself. Causal-role accounts are thus limited in their ability to provide a clear and objective explanation of a trait's function, as they cannot adequately address the issue of accidental effects without compromising their claims.

Etiological accounts, on the other hand, stand out for their explanatory force in vindicating the utility of functional claims. By citing a trait's selected effect, these accounts answer the fundamental historical question of why the trait is present in the first place. This is a crucial aspect of understanding biological function, as it highlights the adaptive significance and evolutionary pressures that have shaped the trait's development. In contrast, purely causal-role accounts can only describe what a trait currently does, without providing insight into its underlying historical context. The etiological approach thus offers a more complete and nuanced understanding of biological function, one that is grounded in the evolutionary history of the trait.

Knowledge acquired through testimony cannot be reduced to knowledge grounded in the hearer's own perception, memory, and inductive inference. This is because the verification of the track record of sources on whom ordinary belief depends is a task that no individual can accomplish independently. As Coady argued, most people's beliefs rely on a vast array of sources, including experts, authorities, and everyday witnesses, and it is practically impossible for an individual to verify the credibility of more than a small fraction of these sources. This limitation renders a reductionist justification of testimony unavailable in practice, as the hearer cannot independently verify the accuracy of the testimony they receive. As a result, knowledge acquired through testimony must be understood as a unique form of knowledge that cannot be reduced to the hearer's own cognitive faculties.

Moreover, young children acquire vast bodies of knowledge through testimony before they possess the inferential resources required for testimonial justification. Children learn about the world around them through language, social interactions, and interactions with their environment, and they often rely on the testimony of their caregivers and other authority figures. However, at this stage in their development, children lack the cognitive maturity and inferential abilities necessary to critically evaluate the testimony they receive, assess the credibility of the sources, or draw inferences from the information. Therefore, their knowledge cannot be reduced to the hearer's own perception, memory, and inductive inference, as they are still in the process of developing these cognitive abilities. Instead, their knowledge is acquired through a process of social learning, where they absorb information and beliefs from their environment and the people around them.

The division of cognitive labor in contemporary science also renders knowledge irreducibly dependent on testimonial trust. As Hardwig's analysis of the division of cognitive labor reveals, researchers in various fields often rely on the work and results of colleagues in other areas of study, without having the necessary expertise or resources to personally verify these results. For example, a physicist may rely on the mathematical calculations of a mathematician or the experimental results of a biologist, without having the ability to personally check the underlying assumptions or methodology. This reliance on the work of others is a fundamental aspect of modern scientific inquiry, where the cumulative knowledge of a community of experts is essential for advancing our understanding of the world. In this context, knowledge acquired through testimony cannot be reduced to the hearer's own perception, memory, and inductive inference, as the verification of the results of others is a collective effort that requires a high degree of trust and cooperation.

Idealized scientific models that contain known falsehoods can provide genuine understanding of natural phenomena by isolating the difference-making factors of a phenomenon. These idealizations, such as frictionless planes, infinite populations, and point masses, deliberately remove factors that do not alter the explanatory structure of the phenomenon. This removal allows scientists to focus on the essential components that contribute to the phenomenon, thereby uncovering the underlying patterns and relationships that govern its behavior. For instance, the concept of a frictionless plane is often used in physics to simplify the analysis of motion, by ignoring the effects of friction that can obscure the underlying dynamics of the system. By omitting these details, scientists can concentrate on the fundamental principles that govern the motion, such as the conservation of energy and momentum.

Understanding consists in grasping patterns of counterfactual dependence, which an idealized model can represent accurately even when its literal assumptions are false. Counterfactual dependence refers to the relationships between different components of a system that would have occurred if certain conditions had been different. Idealized models can capture these patterns by abstracting away from the specific details of a system and focusing on the general properties that determine its behavior. For example, the ideal gas law, which assumes that gases consist of point particles in random motion, accurately predicts the behavior of real gases despite the fact that the assumption of point particles is not strictly true. This is because the ideal gas law captures the essential patterns of counterfactual dependence that govern the behavior of gases, even if it does not accurately represent the microscopic details of the system.

Minimal-model explanations, as analyzed by Batterman, account for universal behavior across physically heterogeneous systems precisely because they omit the microscopic details that differ between those systems. These explanations focus on the essential features that determine the behavior of a system, by abstracting away from the specific details that are not essential to the phenomenon. By doing so, they reveal the underlying patterns and relationships that govern the behavior of a wide range of systems, even if the specific systems themselves are quite different. For instance, the Navier-Stokes equations, which describe the behavior of fluids, can be applied to a wide range of systems, from ocean currents to blood flow, despite the fact that the specific details of each system are quite different. This is because the equations capture the essential patterns of counterfactual dependence that govern the behavior of fluids, even if they do not accurately represent the microscopic details of each system.

The distinction between practical knowledge, or knowing how, and propositional knowledge, or knowing that, is essential to understanding the complexities of human knowledge. This distinction is rooted in the idea that practical knowledge is not reducible to propositional knowledge. One of the key arguments in support of this claim is Ryle's regress argument. This argument suggests that if every intelligent performance required first contemplating a proposition, the act of applying that proposition would itself require further propositional knowledge. The problem with this idea is that it generates an infinite regress. If every time an agent applies a proposition to a situation, they need to contemplate another proposition to guide the application of the first proposition, and so on, then we are left with an endless series of propositions that must be contemplated. This regress is problematic because it is difficult to see how such a series of propositions could ever be completed, let alone put into action.

Furthermore, skilled performance involves context-sensitive responsiveness to particular situations that outstrips any finite set of propositions an agent could articulate or endorse. When an expert driver navigates a complex road network, for instance, their performance is guided by a vast array of implicit rules and norms that they may not be able to explicitly articulate. These rules and norms are not reducible to a finite set of propositions, but rather are embedded in the expert's practical knowledge. The expert's ability to respond to changing road conditions, anticipate the actions of other drivers, and adjust their speed and steering accordingly, is a product of their practical knowledge, rather than a set of explicit propositions. This suggests that practical knowledge is a distinct form of knowledge that cannot be reduced to propositional knowledge.

Neuropsychological dissociations also provide evidence that practical and propositional knowledge can come apart. For example, amnesic patients who acquire new motor skills while retaining no explicit memory of having practiced them demonstrate a separation between practical and propositional knowledge. These patients are able to perform complex motor tasks, such as riding a bicycle or playing a musical instrument, despite having no conscious memory of learning these skills. This suggests that practical knowledge, which is essential to skilled performance, can be separated from propositional knowledge, which is often associated with explicit memory and the ability to articulate rules and propositions. The fact that these patients are able to acquire new motor skills despite their lack of explicit memory highlights the importance of practical knowledge in skilled performance, and demonstrates that it is a distinct form of knowledge that cannot be reduced to propositional knowledge.

The loss of biodiversity undermines the long-term stability and functioning of ecosystems by eroding two essential components: the insurance hypothesis and functional redundancy. The insurance hypothesis posits that species differ in their responses to environmental fluctuation, allowing communities with more species to maintain more stable aggregate productivity as conditions change. This is because diverse ecosystems are better equipped to absorb and recover from disturbances, such as droughts or floods. When species with unique traits and adaptations are present, they can compensate for the losses incurred by other species, thereby reducing the risk of community-wide collapse. Conversely, ecosystems with fewer species are more vulnerable to environmental fluctuations, making them more susceptible to extinction and ecosystem instability.

Functional redundancy, a related concept, suggests that several species perform overlapping ecological roles, effectively buffering ecosystem processes against the loss of any single species. This redundancy is particularly evident in ecosystems where multiple species can occupy the same ecological niche, such as pollination or decomposition. When one species is removed, other species can assume its role, minimizing the impact on the ecosystem. However, as species are removed, this buffer erodes, leaving ecosystems increasingly dependent on a smaller number of species to perform essential ecological functions. This reduction in redundancy can lead to a tipping point beyond which the ecosystem's ability to recover from disturbances or maintain its productivity is compromised.

The loss of keystone species can also trigger trophic cascades, demonstrating that the effects of a single extinction can propagate through an entire community. A keystone species is one that has a disproportionate impact on its environment, often through its interactions with other species. When a keystone species declines or becomes extinct, it can release a cascade of effects that reverberate throughout the ecosystem. For example, the decline of sea otters in kelp forests allowed sea urchins to overgraze the kelp, leading to a dramatic decrease in kelp forest productivity. The loss of sea otters had a ripple effect throughout the ecosystem, ultimately impacting the survival of other species that depend on the kelp forest. The loss of keystone species can thus have far-reaching consequences for ecosystem stability and functioning.

During the day, the sky appears blue due to a phenomenon called Rayleigh scattering. This occurs when sunlight interacts with the tiny molecules of gases in the Earth's atmosphere, such as nitrogen and oxygen. The blue wavelengths of light are scattered in all directions by these molecules, while the longer wavelengths of light, like red and orange, continue to travel in a straight line to our eyes, making the sky appear blue.

Ice floats on liquid water because it is less dense than liquid water. This is due to the arrangement of water molecules in ice, which forms a rigid crystal lattice structure. In this structure, water molecules are spaced further apart than in liquid water, making ice about 9% less dense than liquid water. As a result, ice will float on top of liquid water, rather than sinking to the bottom.

A rainbow forms when sunlight passes through water droplets in the air, such as after a rain shower or near a waterfall. The sunlight is refracted, or bent, as it enters the droplet and is split into its individual colors, a process known as dispersion. The different colors are then reflected off the back of the droplet and exit the droplet, appearing as a colorful arc in the sky.

Earth has seasons due to its tilted axis as it orbits the Sun. This tilt, approximately 23.5 degrees, causes different parts of the planet to receive varying amounts of sunlight throughout the year. As Earth rotates, the changing angle of sunlight results in distinct seasons, with the Northern Hemisphere experiencing summer when the axis is tilted towards the Sun and winter when it's tilted away.

Ocean tides are primarily caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon on the Earth's oceans. As the Moon orbits the Earth, its gravitational force causes the water in the oceans to bulge out in two areas: one on the side of the Earth facing the Moon and the other on the opposite side. This results in the rise and fall of the sea level, creating high and low tides.

Bread dough rises due to the action of yeast, a microorganism that ferments the sugars in the dough. As yeast consumes sugars, it produces carbon dioxide gas as a byproduct, which gets trapped in the dough's network of air pockets. This trapped gas causes the dough to expand and rise, giving bread its light and airy texture.

A black hole is a region in space where the gravitational pull is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape. It's formed when a massive star collapses in on itself, causing a massive amount of matter to be compressed into an incredibly small area. This compression creates a massive gravitational field that warps space and time around the black hole.

A metal spoon feels colder than a wooden spoon because it has a higher thermal conductivity, allowing it to efficiently transfer heat away from the hand. This means that the heat from the hand is quickly lost to the metal, making it feel colder. In contrast, the wooden spoon has a lower thermal conductivity and a higher thermal mass, allowing it to retain the heat from the hand for a longer period.

A refrigerator keeps food cold by using a refrigerant to transfer heat from the inside to the outside. The refrigerant, typically a liquid such as Freon, absorbs heat from the food and other contents inside the fridge, causing it to evaporate into a gas. This gas then passes through a compressor, which compresses it into a high-pressure, high-temperature gas that releases heat to the outside. The now-cooled refrigerant gas then passes through an expansion valve, causing it to expand and cool, repeating the cycle.

Photosynthesis is a process that occurs in plants, where they use energy from sunlight to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose, a type of sugar that serves as food for the plant. This process also produces oxygen as a byproduct, which is released into the air. Glucose gives the plant energy to grow, develop, and reproduce, while oxygen is essential for the survival of many living organisms, including humans.

The leaves of many trees change color in autumn due to a reduction in chlorophyll production. This allows other pigments, such as carotenoids (yellow and orange) and anthocyanins (red and purple), to become visible, resulting in the characteristic autumn foliage colors.

Weather refers to the short-term and local conditions of the atmosphere at a specific place and time, such as temperature, humidity, cloudiness, and precipitation. Climate, on the other hand, is the long-term average weather pattern of a region, including temperature, precipitation, and other atmospheric conditions over a significant period, typically 30 years or more. In other words, weather is what's happening today or tomorrow, while climate is the overall trend or average of what happens over a longer period.

This allows the compass to indicate direction and provide a convenient way to navigate.

This means that the same amount of money can buy fewer goods and services than it could before, and that the value of money is eroded. An airplane wing generates lift by using the principle of air pressure difference. As air flows over the curved surface of the wing, it speeds up and becomes thinner, resulting in lower air pressure above the wing. Meanwhile, the air flowing along the flatter bottom surface of the wing slows down and becomes thicker, creating higher air pressure below the wing. This pressure difference creates an upward force, known as lift, that counteracts the weight of the plane and keeps it flying.

def is_palindrome(s: str) -> bool:
    """

    Parameters:
    s (str): The input string to check.

    Returns:
    bool: True if the string reads the same forwards and backwards, False otherwise.
    """

    # Remove non-alphanumeric characters and convert to lowercase
    s = ''.join(filter(str.isalnum, s)).lower()

    # Check if the string is a palindrome by comparing it with its reverse
    return s == s[::-1]

def fizzbuzz(n: int) -> list[str]:
    """
    Function that returns a list of strings for the integers from 1 to `n` inclusive,
    where multiples of both 3 and 5 are replaced by "FizzBuzz", other multiples of 3 by "Fizz",
    other multiples of 5 by "Buzz", and every other number by its decimal string.

    Parameters:
        n (int): The maximum integer to check and include in the list.

    Returns:
        list[str]: A list of strings representing the integers from 1 to `n` (inclusive)
        according to the specified conditions.
    """

    results = []
    for num in range(1, n + 1):
        if num % 3 == 0 and num % 5 == 0:
            results.append("FizzBuzz")
        elif num % 3 == 0:
            results.append("Fizz")
        elif num % 5 == 0:
            results.append("Buzz")
        else:
            results.append(str(num))

    return results

def sieve_primes(n: int) -> list[int]:
    """
    Returns all prime numbers less than or equal to n in increasing order, using the Sieve of Eratosthenes.
    If n is less than 2, returns an empty list.
    """

    if n < 2:
        return []

    primes = [True] * (n + 1)
    primes[0], primes[1] = False, False

    for i in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1):
        if primes[i]:
            start = i * i
            while start <= n:
                primes[start] = False
                start += i

    return [num for num in range(2, n + 1) if primes[num]]
```

This function generates all prime numbers up to a given number `n` using the Sieve of Eratosthenes. The function first checks if `n` is less than 2, and if so, returns an empty list. It then initializes a list of booleans, where `True` represents a prime number and `False` represents a non-prime number.

The function then iterates through numbers starting from 2, checking if the current number is prime (i.e., the corresponding boolean value in the list is `True`). If the current number is prime, it marks all multiples of the current number as non-prime in the list. Finally, the function returns a list of all prime numbers found.

def run_length_encode(s: str) -> str:
    """
    Encodes a string by replacing each maximal run of a repeated character
    with the character followed by the length of the run.

    Parameters:
    s (str): The input string to be encoded.

    Returns:
    str: The encoded string.
    """

    result = []
    current_char, count = s[0], 1

    for char in s[1:]:
        if char == current_char:
            count += 1
        else:
            result.append(current_char * count)
            current_char = char
            count = 1

    # If the last character is not the end of a run, add it to the result
    if count > 1:
        result.append(current_char * count)

    return "".join(result)
```

This function maintains a running count of the current character and appends the count to the result whenever it encounters a new character. It then returns the encoded string by concatenating all the elements in the result list with an empty string (`""`) as the join separator.

import re

def valid_brackets(s: str) -> bool:
    """
    Checks if the given string s has correctly matched and nested brackets.

    Args:
        s (str): The input string containing brackets.

    Returns:
        bool: True if the brackets are correctly nested, False otherwise.
    """

    # Create a regular expression pattern for the bracket types
    pattern = re.compile(r'(\([^{}]*\)|\[[^{}]*\]|\{\{[^{}]*\}\})')

    # Initialize an empty stack
    stack = []

    # Iterate through the string characters
    for char in s:
        # If the character is an opening bracket, push it onto the stack
        if char in '([{':
            stack.append(char)

        # If the character is a closing bracket, check if it has a corresponding opening bracket
        elif char in ')]}' and stack:
            # If the top element in the stack is the corresponding opening bracket, pop it
            opening_bracket = stack.pop()
            # If the stack is empty after popping, the function returns False
            if not stack:
                return False

            # If the stack is not empty but the popped opening bracket doesn't match the current closing bracket, the function returns False
            if (opening_bracket != '(' and char != ')' and opening_bracket != '[' and char != ']' and
                    opening_bracket != '{' and char != '}'):
                return False

    # If the string is processed without returning False, it means all brackets are correctly matched and nested
    return not stack
```

This function uses a regular expression pattern to match and process the brackets in the input string `s`. The stack data structure is used to keep track of the opening brackets and check if they have a corresponding closing bracket. If the stack is empty after processing the string, it means all brackets are correctly matched and nested. If the stack is not empty, it means there is an unmatched or unnested bracket in the string.

def flatten(nested):
    """
    Flattens a nested list by recursively iterating over all elements.
    :param nested: A list of any depth with nested lists and non-list elements.
    :return: A new flat list containing all non-list elements.
    """

    flat_list = []

    def flat_recurse(sublist):
        for element in sublist:
            if isinstance(element, list):
                flat_recurse(element)
            else:
                flat_list.append(element)

    flat_recurse(nested)
    return flat_list
```

The function `flatten` takes a nested list as an argument and returns a new flat list containing all non-list elements. It uses recursion to traverse the list and its nested lists, appending non-list elements to the `flat_list`. The `flat_recurse` helper function is defined to handle the recursive traversal of the nested list.

def merge_intervals(intervals: list[tuple[int, int]]) -> list[tuple[int, int]]:
    """
    Merge overlapping or touching intervals into a single sorted list.
    Input: list of closed intervals (start, end), in any order.
    Output: minimal list of merged intervals sorted by start.
    """

    if not intervals:
        return []

    intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])

    result = [intervals[0]]
    for current in intervals[1:]:
        last = result[-1]
        if last[1] >= current[0]:
            last[1] = max(last[1], current[1])
        else:
            result.append(current)

    return result

```

This function first sorts the input list of intervals by their start points. It then iterates through the sorted intervals, merging any overlapping or touching intervals into a single interval and appending the non-overlapping intervals to a result list. The result list is sorted and returned at the end.

def rotate_matrix(matrix: list[list[int]]) -> list[list[int]]:
    """
    Rotates an n-by-n square matrix 90 degrees clockwise.

    Args:
        matrix (list[list[int]]): A two-dimensional list representing the matrix to rotate.

    Returns:
        list[list[int]]: The rotated matrix.
    """

    n = len(matrix)
    rotated = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]

    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            k = n - 1 - j
            rotated[i][k] = matrix[j][i]

    return rotated

```

In this function, we first create a new list `rotated` to store the rotated matrix with the correct dimensions. We then iterate through the original matrix, using `i` and `j` as indices, and calculate the new indices `k` for the rotated matrix based on the current indices. The value at the new indices is set to the original matrix value at the current indices. The rotated matrix is then returned.

def top_k_words(text: str, k: int) -> list[tuple[str, int]]:
    """
    Returns the top `k` most frequent words in `text`,
    where a word is defined as a maximal run of letters a to z and apostrophes.
    If there are fewer than `k` distinct words, return all of them.
    """

    from collections import Counter, defaultdict

    # Split text into words and count their occurrences
    word_count = Counter(word for word in text.lower().split() if word.isalnum())

    # Store the most common words for fast lookup
    freq_limit = k if k <= len(word_count) else len(word_count)
    most_common = sorted(word_count.mostcommon(freq_limit), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)

    # If there are fewer than k distinct words, return all of them
    return most_common if k >= len(word_count) else most_common[:k]
```

This function uses the `Counter` class from the `collections` module to count the occurrences of each word. It then sorts the most common words in descending order of frequency and, for ties, alphabetically. If there are fewer than `k` distinct words, it returns all of them.

def leftmost_index(arr: list[int], target: int) -> int:
    """
    Binary search to find the leftmost index of a target value in a sorted list,
    with duplicates allowed. Returns -1 if the target is not present.
    """

    left, right = 0, len(arr) - 1

    while left <= right:
        mid = (left + right) // 2
        if arr[mid] == target:
            right = mid - 1
            while right >= 0 and arr[right] == target:
                right -= 1
            return right + 1
        elif arr[mid] < target:
            left = mid + 1
        else:
            right = mid - 1

    return -1

```

This function uses binary search to find the leftmost index of a target value in a sorted list. It starts by initializing the left and right pointers at the beginning and end of the list, respectively. The function then enters a loop where it continuously narrows the search space by either moving the left pointer to the right or the right pointer to the left, depending on whether the current midpoint's value is less than, equal to, or greater than the target value. If the current midpoint's value is equal to the target value, it checks for any potential duplicate occurrences to the left of the midpoint and adjusts the right pointer accordingly. If the target value is not found, it returns -1.

def max_subarray_sum(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    """
    Returns the largest sum of any non-empty contiguous subarray of `nums`.
    Uses Kadane's algorithm. If all numbers are negative, returns the largest single element.
    Raises ValueError if `nums` is empty.
    """

    if not nums:
        raise ValueError("List cannot be empty.")

    max_current = max_global = nums[0]

    for num in nums[1:]:
        max_current = max(num, max_current + num)
        max_global = max(max_global, max_current)

    return max_global

def moving_average(values: list[float], window: int) -> list[float]:
    """
    Calculate the moving average of a list of values, with a specified window size.

    Args:
        values (list[float]): A list of numerical values.
        window (int): The number of contiguous values to average at each step.

    Returns:
        list[float]: A list of moving averages, with the same number of elements as the input list,
                     except if `window` is greater than the length of the input list, in which case an empty list is returned.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If `window` is less than 1.
    """

    if window < 1:
        raise ValueError("Window size must be at least 1.")

    if len(values) < window:
        return []

    total, count = 0.0, 0
    result = []

    for value in values:
        total += value
        count += 1

        if count >= window:
            result.append(total / window)
            total -= values[count - window]

    return result
```

def edit_distance(a, b):
    """
    Returns the Levenshtein distance between two strings, the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, and substitutions needed to turn `a` into `b`.

    Parameters:
    a (str): The first string.
    b (str): The second string.

    Returns:
    int: The Levenshtein distance between `a` and `b`.
    """

    len_a = len(a)
    len_b = len(b)

    matrix = [[0] * (len_b + 1) for _ in range(len_a + 1)]

    for i in range(len_a + 1):
        matrix[i][0] = i

    for j in range(len_b + 1):
        matrix[0][j] = j

    for i in range(1, len_a + 1):
        for j in range(1, len_b + 1):
            cost = 0 if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1] else 1
            matrix[i][j] = min(
                matrix[i - 1][j] + 1,
                matrix[i][j - 1] + 1,
                matrix[i - 1][j - 1] + cost,
            )

    return matrix[len_a][len_b]

```

def shortest_paths(graph: dict[str, list[tuple[str, int]]], source: str) -> dict[str, int]:
    """
    Implement Dijkstra's algorithm using heapq to find the shortest paths from a given source node in a weighted graph.

    Args:

        source (str): The starting node for the shortest path calculation.

    Returns:
        dict[str, int]: A dictionary mapping each node reachable from the source node, including the source node itself, to the length of its shortest path.
    """

    import heapq as hp

    distances = {source: 0}
    frontier = hp.heappushpop(hp.PriorityQueue(), (0, source))

    while frontier:
        current_distance, current_node = frontier.pop()
        current_node_distance = distances[current_node]

        for neighbor, weight in graph[current_node]:
            distance_to_neighbor = current_distance + weight

            if neighbor not in distances or distance_to_neighbor < distances[neighbor]:
                distances[neighbor] = distance_to_neighbor
                hp.heappush(frontier, (distance_to_neighbor, neighbor))

    return distances

2. The bacteria population doubles every 20 minutes. So, to find out how many doubling periods occur in 2 hours, we divide the total minutes by the doubling period: 120 minutes / 20 minutes = 6 doubling periods.
3. Since the population doubles each time, we can calculate the number of bacteria after each doubling period:
   - Initially, there are 150 bacteria.
   - After the first doubling period (20 minutes), the population is 150 * 2 = 300 bacteria.
   - After the second doubling period (40 minutes), the population is 300 * 2 = 600 bacteria.
   - This pattern continues until we reach the final doubling period, which occurs at the end of the 2-hour interval.
4. After six doubling periods, the bacteria population will be 150 * 2^6 = 150 * 64 = 9600.

Answer: 9600

To find the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand of an analog clock at 3:40, we can use the following steps:

1. First, let's understand that the hour hand moves 360 degrees in 12 hours, while the minute hand moves 360 degrees in 60 minutes. In 60 minutes, the hour hand moves approximately 5 degrees (since it covers 360 degrees in 12*5 = 60 minutes).

2. At 3:40, the hour hand is pointing towards the third hour mark (3 o'clock), and the minute hand is pointing to the 40th minute mark.

3. In this case, the hour hand has moved 1/12 of a full circle (or 30 degrees) from the 12 o'clock position, while the minute hand has moved 40/60 of a full circle (or 40/6 * 360 = 60 degrees).

4. Now, we need to find the difference in degrees between these two positions, which is the angle between the hands. To do this, we subtract the angle of the hour hand from the angle of the minute hand: 60 - 30 = 30 degrees.

Answer: 30 degrees

First, let's consider the single-digit numbers (1, 2, 3, ..., 9). Out of these, only the number 7 itself contains a digit 7. So, there is 1 number that meets our criteria in this range.

Next, let's move on to two-digit numbers (10, 11, ..., 99). Here, we need to find numbers that have a digit 7 in the tens place, hundreds place, or both. However, since we are double-counting numbers like 707 and 770, we should subtract those duplicates, which gives us 90 + 90 - 10 = 170 numbers.

For three-digit numbers (100, 101, ..., 999), we have three possible places for a digit 7: hundreds, tens, and units. There are 90 numbers with a 7 in the hundreds place (700, 701, ..., 799). For each of those numbers, there are 10 numbers with a 7 in the tens place (7000, 7001, ..., 7099). Again, we should subtract duplicates, so 90 * 9 - 10 = 810 numbers.

Putting it all together, we have:

1 single-digit number (7)
170 two-digit numbers (70, 71, ..., 79 and their duplicates)
890 three-digit numbers (700, 701, ..., 799 and their duplicates)

The total number of integers from 1 to 1000 inclusive that contain at least one digit 7 in their decimal representation is:

1 (single-digit number) + 170 (two-digit numbers) + 890 (three-digit numbers) = 1061

Answer: 1061

Adequate sleep each night plays a pivotal role in shaping our daily functioning, as it significantly impacts various aspects of our cognitive, emotional, and physical well-being. This article will delve into three specific effects of sleep deprivation and the benefits of getting enough sleep, focusing on sharper focus and memory, better mood and emotional control, and improved physical energy.

Firstly, sleep is essential for maintaining cognitive functions such as focus and memory. During sleep, our brains consolidate and process information from the day, strengthening neural connections and enhancing our ability to recall memories and think clearly. Conversely, sleep deprivation hampers these processes, leading to difficulties in concentration, problem-solving, and memory retention. Adequate sleep ensures that our brains are well-rested and primed to tackle the challenges of the day with a sharper focus and a more effective memory.

Secondly, sleep has a profound impact on our emotional well-being and emotional control. Lack of sleep can lead to increased irritability, mood swings, and decreased ability to cope with stress. This is because sleep plays a crucial role in regulating our emotions by helping to maintain a balance of neurotransmitters in the brain, such as serotonin, which is involved in mood regulation. Adequate sleep ensures that these neurotransmitters are balanced, allowing us to maintain a more stable emotional state and exhibit better emotional control throughout the day.

Lastly, getting enough sleep is crucial for our physical energy levels. Sleep is the time when our bodies repair and rejuvenate, restoring energy levels and building muscle tissue. Lack of sleep can lead to feelings of fatigue, decreased motivation, and reduced physical performance. On the other hand, adequate sleep ensures that our bodies are well-rested and ready to tackle physical tasks with increased energy and stamina.

In conclusion, getting enough sleep each night is essential for maintaining optimal functioning the following day. Adequate sleep allows our brains to consolidate and process information more effectively, enabling us to focus better, remember more, and think more clearly. It also contributes to a more stable emotional state and improved emotional control. Furthermore, it ensures that our bodies are well-rested and prepared for physical exertion, providing us with the necessary energy to tackle the challenges of the day. Prioritizing sleep is, therefore, a vital investment in our overall health and well-being.

Opting for home-cooked meals over dining out is a choice that significantly enhances one's health, wallet, and skillset. This preference is grounded in three primary reasons: the ability to regulate food content, financial savings, and the acquisition of valuable life skills.

Firstly, the paramount advantage of home cooking lies in the control it affords over the ingredients used. In contrast to restaurant meals where the exact composition of each dish may be unknown, home-cooked meals allow for precise selection of ingredients based on individual dietary preferences and nutritional requirements. For instance, those with dietary restrictions such as lactose intolerance or gluten sensitivity can tailor their meals to avoid these allergens, ensuring a healthier diet. Moreover, home cooks can prioritize fresh, whole foods over processed alternatives, thereby reducing the intake of unhealthy additives, preservatives, and trans fats.

Secondly, home cooking is a financially prudent decision for many households. Eating out regularly can quickly accumulate costs, with the price of a meal often exceeding the expense of preparing a comparable meal at home. By shopping for ingredients at their convenience and leveraging sales, home cooks can create nutritious meals at a fraction of the cost of dining out. In this way, home cooking serves as a means of maximizing both health and financial well-being.

Lastly, cooking at home offers an opportunity to acquire and hone essential life skills. Aside from the practical ability to prepare meals, home cooking fosters an understanding of food preparation, portion control, and nutrition. These skills are invaluable for maintaining a balanced diet and overall health. Furthermore, cooking can serve as a means of personal expression and a source of relaxation, fostering a positive relationship with food and promoting a healthier lifestyle.

In summary, cooking meals at home offers numerous benefits, including the ability to control food content, financial savings, and the opportunity to develop valuable life skills. By taking control of their diet and embracing the art of home cooking, individuals can not only improve their health but also cultivate a deeper appreciation for the food they consume.

A daily routine, when cultivated and adhered to, serves as a vital weapon against the insidious encroachment of stress in our lives. By establishing a predictable structure, we effectively disarm the mental burden of constant decision-making, thus reducing stress levels.

In the hustle and bustle of modern life, the mind is incessantly bombarded with a myriad of choices. Each day presents a multitude of decisions, from what to wear, to what to eat, to how to spend our time. While these choices may seem minor, they cumulatively contribute to a mental load that can be exhausting. A routine, however, streamlines these choices, allowing us to focus our mental energy on more pressing matters. This simplification of decision-making process, in turn, leads to a reduction in mental stress.

Moreover, a consistent daily routine has a profound impact on our sleep quality. By regulating our body clock, we allow our bodies to acclimatize to a regular sleep-wake cycle. This regularity aids in the production of melatonin, the hormone responsible for regulating sleep-wake patterns. A well-rested mind is less prone to stress, as it has the necessary energy to face the challenges of the day. Conversely, sleep deprivation can lead to increased stress levels, exacerbating the symptoms of anxiety and depression.

Lastly, a daily routine facilitates the integration of exercise and self-care into our lives. Regular physical activity is a well-documented stress reducer, as it stimulates the production of endorphins, the body's natural mood lifters. Additionally, self-care practices such as meditation, journaling, or even taking a few minutes to enjoy a cup of coffee can help reduce stress levels by promoting mindfulness and emotional well-being.

By embedding these stress-reducing practices into our daily routine, we create a proactive approach to stress management. Rather than reacting to stress as it arises, we are able to proactively address it, fostering a healthier, less stressful lifestyle. Thus, a daily routine, when intentionally designed, serves as a powerful ally in the fight against stress.

Embracing the practice of budgeting each month is not merely an exercise in financial management; it is a pathway to a more secure and stress-free financial future. Here are three compelling reasons why learning to budget your money is a worthwhile endeavor:

1. Prevent overspending: One of the most immediate benefits of budgeting is that it helps you avoid overspending by keeping track of your income and expenses. By setting clear limits on your spending, you can ensure that you are living within your means, rather than constantly struggling to make ends meet. This not only prevents you from accumulating unnecessary debt, but also allows you to enjoy the things you truly value, without the guilt or anxiety that comes from overspending.

2. Build savings over time: Budgeting isn't just about controlling your spending—it's also about planning for the future. By setting aside a portion of your income each month, you can build a savings cushion that will provide you with financial stability and security. This cushion can serve as a safety net in the event of unexpected expenses, such as car repairs or medical bills, or it can be used to fund long-term goals, such as buying a home or starting a business. By consistently saving, you can create a financial foundation that will support you throughout your life.

3. Reduces financial stress: Perhaps the most significant advantage of budgeting is the peace of mind it offers. By having a clear understanding of your financial situation, you can eliminate the stress and worry that often accompanies financial uncertainty. Instead of fretting over bills or living in fear of unexpected expenses, you can approach your finances with a sense of confidence and control. This allows you to enjoy your life more fully, knowing that you are making the most of your resources and planning for the future.

In essence, budgeting is not a chore or a burden—it is an investment in your financial well-being. By taking the time to learn and practice budgeting, you can prevent overspending, build savings, and reduce financial stress, ultimately leading to a more secure and stress-free financial future. So, I encourage you to give budgeting a try—you may find that it is one of the most valuable skills you can acquire.

A significant contributing factor to enhancing one's wellbeing lies in the conscious decision to limit the time spent on social media. This choice promotes a healthier mental state by addressing three fundamental aspects: the prevention of constant social comparison, the creation of opportunities for more gratifying offline activities, and the improvement of sleep quality due to reduced evening screen exposure.

Firstly, social media platforms are designed to create an illusion of a flawless, idealized life, encouraging users to compare their own lives with those of others. This constant social comparison can lead to feelings of inadequacy, envy, and dissatisfaction, negatively impacting self-esteem and overall wellbeing. By limiting social media usage, individuals can avoid the relentless cycle of comparison and instead focus on their personal growth and achievements.

Secondly, the time spent on social media is time taken away from engaging in offline activities that foster genuine connections, personal development, and happiness. Engaging in hobbies, reading, exercising, or spending quality time with loved ones can bring a sense of fulfillment, purpose, and joy that often eludes those absorbed in the digital world. By reducing social media consumption, individuals open up the possibility of investing in offline activities that nurture their wellbeing and personal growth.

Lastly, excessive exposure to screens, particularly in the evening, can disrupt sleep patterns and quality. The blue light emitted from screens suppresses melatonin, a hormone essential for regulating sleep-wake cycles, leading to poor sleep quality, daytime fatigue, and increased risk of various health issues. By spending less time on social media, especially in the hours leading up to bedtime, individuals can promote better sleep hygiene and enjoy the restorative benefits of a good night's sleep, thus improving their wellbeing.

In conclusion, the judicious use of social media can lead to a marked improvement in wellbeing. By reducing constant social comparison, creating opportunities for more fulfilling offline activities, and improving sleep quality, individuals can cultivate a more balanced, healthy, and enjoyable life. Embracing short breaks during extended work sessions can significantly enhance productivity and overall output. This strategy is rooted in the understanding that the human brain, like a powerful engine, needs periodic respite to maintain optimal performance and prevent burnout.

Firstly, brief pauses prevent mental fatigue from accumulating, thereby safeguarding cognitive function and productivity. The brain's capacity for focused, high-level thinking is finite, and extended periods of concentration can lead to a decline in performance, often referred to as the "mental fatigue" effect. By taking short breaks, workers can give their brains a much-needed rest, allowing them to return to their tasks with renewed focus and energy. This cycle of work and rest not only ensures that the brain is functioning at its best but also prevents the accumulation of mental fatigue, which can lead to mistakes and decreased efficiency.

Secondly, stepping away from a problem often leads to better solutions when one returns. This phenomenon, known as the incubation effect, occurs when the subconscious mind continues to work on a problem even when the conscious mind is focused elsewhere. By taking a break from a challenging task, individuals allow their subconscious minds to process the information and potentially come up with innovative solutions or approaches. This process is akin to a chef tasting a dish, setting it aside, and then returning with fresh perspectives to fine-tune the flavors and textures.

Lastly, regular breaks maintain motivation across the full work period. Sustaining motivation throughout an extended work session can be challenging, as the brain craves variety and novelty. By incorporating short breaks, workers introduce variety into their workdays, preventing monotony and fostering a sense of excitement and anticipation for the next task. Furthermore, taking breaks can help individuals reflect on their progress, set new goals, and recharge their motivation, ensuring that they remain engaged and dedicated to their work for the entire duration of the work period.

In conclusion, short breaks during long work sessions can lead to increased productivity, better problem-solving, and sustained motivation. By preventing mental fatigue, encouraging incubation, and maintaining motivation, these breaks help individuals get more done overall, ultimately leading to a more efficient and effective workforce.
